skills.content:
---
name: allocate-medallion-responsibilities
description: >-
  Assign datasets and transformations to Bronze, Silver, and Gold and select a
  justified modeling approach for each. Use when planning a medallion subject
  area or resolving where validation, canonical entities, history, dimensions,
  facts, and aggregates belong.
---
# Allocate medallion responsibilities

## Inputs
Read the requirements, available source behavior, logical model, existing layer contracts, and consumer queries. Preserve established architecture unless evidence supports a proposed change.

## Procedure
1. Separate model detail from storage layers. Conceptual, logical, and physical models describe design detail; Bronze, Silver, and Gold describe data-product responsibilities.
2. Assign source-faithful, replayable capture to Bronze; validated detailed data and reusable integration to Silver; business-facing analytical products to Gold. Gold may include atomic facts and dimensions as well as aggregates.
3. Place each transformation once: parsing, type conversion, source deduplication, identity resolution, relationship resolution, history capture, business derivation, and aggregation. State when downstream products reuse the result.
4. Choose the scheme per product. Consider relational/canonical structures for reusable integration, dimensional structures for analytical navigation, nested structures for suitable collections, and time-based patterns when audit/integration requirements justify their complexity. Do not require Data Vault, universal 3NF, or a star for every product.
5. Preserve source history needed by downstream consumers. A current-state Silver table alone cannot support a later reconstruction of changes it discarded. Specify a retained event/history source or explicitly limit supported history.
6. Define each layer's incoming grain, outgoing grain, keys, quality promises, rejected-record treatment, access boundary, retention, and rebuild source. Reconcile counts across transformations that split, filter, or aggregate rows.
7. Separate reference, operational metadata, and semantic assets where existing conventions require it; do not invent additional layers merely to hold a new object.

## Output
Produce a matrix with source/product, layer, purpose, grain, identity, transformations, history, quality contract, consumers, and rebuild path. Record major scheme decisions and rejected alternatives with requirement-based reasons.

## Completion checks
Ensure every transformation has an owner, every derived product has an upstream source, and every history requirement has a retained basis. Do not force one source table to become exactly one table in every layer.

## Basis
Adapt the scheme and physical-design principles in DAMA-DMBOK2 chapter 5, printed pp. 136–158, using the layer responsibilities in https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion .

skills.name: assess-platform-and-tool-selection
skills.description: Run a defensible platform or tool selection: requirements, a weighted scoring matrix, open table format choice (Delta, Iceberg, Hudi), build vs buy, a proof-of-concept plan with pass/fail criteria, lock-in and exit cost, and a TCO structure. Use when choosing a lakehouse platform, catalog, table format, ingestion/orchestration/quality/BI tool, or when someone proposes replacing one.
skills.content:
---
name: assess-platform-and-tool-selection
description: >-
  Run a defensible platform or tool selection: requirements, a weighted scoring
  matrix, open table format choice (Delta, Iceberg, Hudi), build vs buy, a
  proof-of-concept plan with pass/fail criteria, lock-in and exit cost, and a
  TCO structure. Use when choosing a lakehouse platform, catalog, table format,
  ingestion/orchestration/quality/BI tool, or when someone proposes replacing
  one.
---
# Assess platform and tool selection

## Inputs
Business drivers and constraints, current stack and skills, workload inventory (plan-cost-and-capacity), security/regulatory needs (design-security-and-access-model), cloud and region requirements, procurement rules, and timeline. These decisions are hard to reverse; treat them as one-way doors.

## Procedure
1. **Frame the decision** as an ADR draft: problem, scope, constraints, decision date, decision owner.
2. **Write requirements** split into must-haves (pass/fail gates) and weighted criteria. Candidates failing any must-have are dropped before scoring.
3. **Long-list then short-list** to 2-3 options, always including "keep current / improve current" as a baseline.
4. **Agree weights before scoring** with stakeholders, so scores cannot be tuned to a favorite.
5. **Score from evidence** (docs, references, POC results), not vendor slides. Record the evidence per cell.
6. **Run a time-boxed POC** (2-6 weeks) on real data and real workloads against pre-agreed criteria.
7. **Build the TCO** over 3-5 years with ranges.
8. **Assess lock-in and exit cost.**
9. **Present** with explain-tradeoffs-to-business; publish the ADR with publish-lakehouse-docs-to-repo (status Proposed until the owner accepts).

## Weighted scoring matrix template
| Criterion | Weight % | Option A score (1-5) | A evidence | Option B | B evidence | Baseline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fit to workloads (SQL, streaming, ML) | 20 | | | | | |
| Governance and security | 15 | | | | | |
| Performance on POC benchmarks | 15 | | | | | |
| TCO (3-5 yr, expected) | 15 | | | | | |
| Openness / exit cost | 10 | | | | | |
| Team skills and hiring market | 10 | | | | | |
| Ecosystem / integrations | 10 | | | | | |
| Vendor viability and support | 5 | | | | | |
| **Weighted total** | 100 | | | | | |
Scale: 1 = does not meet, 3 = meets, 5 = clearly exceeds with evidence. Run a sensitivity check: if shifting any weight by +/-5 points changes the winner, call the result close and lean on POC evidence and exit cost.

## Open table format comparison (verify current versions before deciding)
| Aspect | Delta Lake | Apache Iceberg | Apache Hudi |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Strongest ecosystem | Databricks, Spark; broad readers via Delta Kernel | Broadest multi-engine support (Spark, Trino, Flink, Snowflake, Athena, BigQuery) | Spark/Flink upsert-heavy pipelines |
| Strengths | Mature on Databricks, liquid clustering, deletion vectors, CDF | Hidden partitioning, partition evolution, REST catalog standard | Record-level upserts, incremental pulls, merge-on-read |
| Interop | "Iceberg reads" (UniForm, IcebergCompatV2) generates Iceberg metadata for Delta tables | Native in many engines | XTable/interop projects |
Decision rules: default to the platform's native format; choose Iceberg when several engines must write the same tables or multi-vendor portability is a stated requirement; choose Hudi mainly for existing Hudi estates or very upsert-heavy streaming on non-Databricks Spark. The **catalog** (Unity Catalog, Polaris, Glue, Nessie) often matters more for lock-in than the file format.

## Build vs buy rules
| Lean buy/managed when | Lean build/open source when |
| --- | --- |
| Capability is commodity (ingestion connectors, orchestration, BI) | Capability is differentiating for the business |
| Team is small or lacks on-call depth | Team can run and patch it 24x7 |
| Time-to-value matters more than unit cost | Scale makes managed unit pricing dominant |
| Compliance certifications needed quickly | Strict data residency/customization not available in products |
Count the full cost of build: engineers to build and maintain (often the biggest line), on-call, upgrades, security patching.

## POC plan template
| Item | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Scope | 2-3 representative workloads (e.g. one heavy batch, one BI concurrency, one streaming/CDC) |
| Data | Real or production-shaped volume, including the largest table |
| Success criteria | Measurable, agreed upfront: e.g. nightly batch < X min, p95 BI query < Y s at Z concurrent users, row/column security works with IdP groups, CDC lag < N min |
| Cost capture | Actual compute consumed per workload from billing data |
| Team test | Two engineers build a pipeline end to end; record friction |
| Exit test | Export tables and metadata; read them from another engine |
| Timebox | 2-6 weeks; decision meeting date fixed |

## TCO structure (3-5 years, low/expected/high)
Platform compute; storage; network/egress; licenses and support; third-party tools; people (build, run, on-call, training); migration one-time (plan-migration-from-legacy-warehouse); parallel-run double costs; exit cost. Pull prices from vendor pricing pages and quotes with dates; label any illustration as example figures.

## Lock-in and exit cost checklist
- Data in an open format in your own cloud storage account?
- Metadata/catalog exportable (schemas, grants, lineage)?
- Code portable (ANSI SQL, Spark, dbt) or proprietary (vendor-only functions, notebooks, procedural language)?
- Contract: commit terms, egress fees, renewal caps, termination rights.
- Estimate exit effort in person-weeks by layer (data, pipelines, semantic layer, BI, security).

## Worked example
Choosing a table format for a company on Databricks that also lets a partner team query with Trino. Must-haves: ACID, governed by Unity Catalog. Options: Delta native, Delta with Iceberg reads (UniForm), Iceberg managed tables. POC showed Trino reads work through Iceberg REST. Decision: Delta with Iceberg reads (UniForm) enabled, revisit if external writers are needed. ADR records the exit path.

## Anti-patterns
- Weights set after scores are known.
- POC on toy data or vendor-run demos only.
- TCO that omits people and migration.
- Comparing list price to list price without discounts and real usage.
- Treating table format as the whole lock-in story while code and catalog are proprietary.

## Output
ADR, requirements with must-haves, scored matrix with evidence, POC report, TCO ranges, exit-cost assessment, recommendation.

## Completion checks
- Weights agreed and dated before scoring.
- Every score cell has evidence.
- POC criteria were written before the POC and results reported against them.
- TCO includes people, migration, and exit with ranges and dated price sources.
- Baseline "keep current" option was scored.

## Basis
- Delta Lake docs: https://docs.delta.io/index.html
- Apache Iceberg spec: https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/
- Apache Hudi docs: https://hudi.apache.org/docs/overview/
- Databricks Iceberg reads (UniForm): https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/delta/iceberg-reads
- Apache XTable: https://xtable.apache.org/
- Amazon 2015 shareholder letter, one-way vs two-way door decisions (SEC filing): https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1018724/000119312516530910/d168744dex991.htm
- ADR format, Michael Nygard: https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions

skills.name: build-conceptual-data-model
skills.description: Build a business-facing conceptual model with clear entity definitions and relationship cardinalities. Use when defining subject-area boundaries, discussing how business concepts relate, or producing an ERD before logical table design.
skills.content:
---
name: build-conceptual-data-model
description: >-
  Build a business-facing conceptual model with clear entity definitions and
  relationship cardinalities. Use when defining subject-area boundaries,
  discussing how business concepts relate, or producing an ERD before logical
  table design.
---
# Build a conceptual data model

## Inputs
Read the requirements, business vocabulary, existing enterprise model, and relevant source evidence. Treat source tables as evidence, not automatic business entities.

## Procedure
1. Identify the principal business nouns and the verbs connecting them. Distinguish people or organizations, resources, categories, events, and measurements.
2. Write a concise definition and one illustrative instance for each entity. Explain its inclusion and exclusion boundaries. Resolve ambiguous terms such as client, institution, customer, and offering through business meaning.
3. State each relationship in both directions. Specify minimum and maximum participation at each end: zero or one, exactly one, zero or many, or one or many. Record the time context when cardinality changes over time.
4. Identify recursive, many-to-many, and ternary relationships explicitly. Do not replace a three-party business rule with independent pairs unless that preserves the rule.
5. Introduce a supertype, subtype, or party/role pattern only when requirements justify shared identity or attributes. State whether subtypes overlap and whether they cover every supertype instance.
6. Reconcile the local business view with enterprise terminology. Choose a consistent notation; use a compact Mermaid ER diagram when appropriate and accompany it with a relationship table.
7. Walk through representative and boundary scenarios. Record conflicting rules as questions with owners. Mark an uncertain relationship as proposed in the accompanying table.

## Output
Produce the conceptual diagram, entity glossary, bidirectional relationship/cardinality table, requirement links, and unresolved rules. Keep physical schemas, data types, storage layout, surrogate keys, and ingestion metadata out of this model.

## Completion checks
Ensure every relationship has a business verb and defined participation. Confirm that the diagram and written rules agree. Use scoped views for a large subject area instead of one unreadable diagram. Do not invent business sign-off.

## Basis
DAMA-DMBOK2 chapter 5, printed pp. 127–132, 145–146, and 153–154. Relational relationship rules and dimensional navigation paths serve different purposes; label the scheme used.

skills.name: design-bronze-record-contract
skills.description: Design the record shape and replay contract for a Bronze dataset. Use when landing JSON, events, snapshots, or CDC into Databricks and deciding payload preservation, delivery identity, provenance, drift, and deletion semantics.
skills.content:
---
name: design-bronze-record-contract
description: >-
  Design the record shape and replay contract for a Bronze dataset. Use when
  landing JSON, events, snapshots, or CDC into Databricks and deciding payload
  preservation, delivery identity, provenance, drift, and deletion semantics.
---
# Design a Bronze record contract

## Inputs
Read actual source samples or schemas, delivery behavior, source identity rules, ingestion conventions, retention needs, and downstream history requirements. Do not invent JSON paths or source guarantees.

## Procedure
1. Define one landed row: delivered event, source row version, snapshot row, or document. Separate delivery identity from business identity; a repeated delivery is not automatically a new business event.
2. Specify a source-faithful payload and provenance envelope. Include source/instance namespace, file or stream coordinates where available, ingestion timestamp, extraction/run identifier, schema version, and source operation/sequence when supplied.
3. Choose raw text, VARIANT, STRUCT, or other payload representation from fidelity and runtime needs. If byte-exact replay is required, preserve original bytes or a durable source object reference; parsed JSON alone is not byte-exact evidence.
4. Keep source event time, source modification/effective time, and ingestion time separate. Record timestamp units, time-zone assumptions, and precision. Do not infer event order from ingestion order.
5. Document duplicate deliveries, out-of-order records, snapshot completeness, tombstones, partial updates, and missing fields. Absence from an incremental feed is not evidence of deletion.
6. Define handling for unreadable records and schema drift. Preserve recoverable evidence and route failures with a reason; avoid silent loss during casting or parsing.
7. Specify replay inputs, retention limits, and the reconciliation unit. Keep business survivorship and analytical derivations in their assigned downstream layer.

## Output
Produce the Bronze grain, payload/envelope specification, observed source-path inventory, delivery and identity contract, drift policy, rejection policy, and replay/reconciliation design. Distinguish real source fields from proposed metadata columns.

## Completion checks
Show how to trace a downstream row to the original delivery. Demonstrate how a duplicate delivery and a genuine correction remain distinguishable. State any recovery limitations caused by source retention or missing sequences.

## Basis
Apply DAMA-DMBOK2 chapter 5's event, canonical-message, and lineage principles (printed pp. 127, 148, 153) to Bronze responsibilities documented at https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion .

skills.name: design-data-quality-and-observability
skills.description: Design data quality rules and monitoring for lakehouse products: quality dimensions, expectation tiers (warn, quarantine, fail), freshness, volume, schema and distribution monitors, SLOs, incident severity and runbooks. Use when building or hardening a pipeline, writing a data contract, after a data incident, or when consumers ask "can I trust this table".
skills.content:
---
name: design-data-quality-and-observability
description: >-
  Design data quality rules and monitoring for lakehouse products: quality
  dimensions, expectation tiers (warn, quarantine, fail), freshness, volume,
  schema and distribution monitors, SLOs, incident severity and runbooks. Use
  when building or hardening a pipeline, writing a data contract, after a data
  incident, or when consumers ask "can I trust this table".
---
# Design data quality and observability

## Inputs
Data contracts (document-model-contracts-and-lineage), table grain and keys, consumer criticality (who breaks if this is wrong), freshness requirements, history of incidents, the layering approach (medallion, Data Vault, Kimball marts, or other), and the orchestration/alerting tools in use.

## Procedure
1. **Rank tables by criticality**: Tier 1 (exec/regulatory/revenue reporting, customer-facing), Tier 2 (operational analytics), Tier 3 (exploratory). Effort follows the tier.
2. **Pick dimensions per table** from the table below; write at least one rule for completeness, uniqueness, validity, and timeliness on every Tier 1 table.
3. **Assign each rule a tier** (warn, quarantine, fail) using the decision rules.
4. **Place rules by layer.** Ingestion/raw layer: structural checks only (parseable, schema, not-null on keys) and never drop data. Integration/conformed layer: validity, uniqueness, referential integrity, quarantine bad rows. Consumption layer: business reconciliation and metric sanity.
5. **Add table monitors**: freshness, volume, schema change, distribution drift (thresholds below).
6. **Set SLOs** per Tier 1/2 table and publish them in the contract.
7. **Wire alerts and ownership.** Every alert routes to an owning team channel/on-call, not a person.
8. **Write the runbook** and severity table; rehearse once.
9. **Review monthly**: noisy rules (fire > weekly with no action) get tuned or removed.

## Quality dimensions
| Dimension | Example rule |
| --- | --- |
| Completeness | `customer_id IS NOT NULL`; null rate of `email` < 2% |
| Uniqueness | one row per `order_id` per load |
| Validity | `order_status IN (...)`; `amount >= 0`; date parses |
| Consistency / referential | every `fact.customer_sk` exists in `dim_customer` |
| Accuracy / reconciliation | daily revenue within 0.5% of source system total |
| Timeliness | table updated within SLO |

## Expectation tiers
| Tier | Behavior | Use when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Warn | Load all rows, record metric, alert above threshold | Rule is soft or newly introduced (run 2-4 weeks as warn before promoting) |
| Quarantine | Route failing rows to `<table>_quarantine` with reason; load the rest | Row-level defects where partial data is better than none |
| Fail | Stop the pipeline; nothing published | Key uniqueness, schema break, reconciliation outside tolerance on Tier 1, or > X% rows failing (e.g. > 5%) |

Databricks Lakeflow pipelines (formerly Delta Live Tables) map these to `EXPECT` / `dp.expect` (warn), `EXPECT ... ON VIOLATION DROP ROW` / `dp.expect_or_drop` (drop; pair with a quarantine table by inverting the rule), and `ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE` / `dp.expect_or_fail` (fail). Elsewhere: dbt tests (`severity: warn|error`), Great Expectations, Soda, or Snowflake Data Metric Functions.

## Monitor thresholds (starting points; tune on 4-8 weeks of history)
| Monitor | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Freshness | Alert when `now - max(loaded_at)` > SLO; page when > 2x SLO |
| Volume | Alert when row count outside +/-3 standard deviations of trailing 28 days for same weekday, or 0 rows |
| Schema | Alert on any added/dropped/retyped column vs contract; fail on dropped key column |
| Distribution | Alert when null rate, distinct count, or mean of key measures shifts > 3 sd, or category share changes > 20 points |

## Quality rule YAML template
```yaml
table: prod.silver_sales.orders
owner: grp_sales_data_eng
criticality: tier1
slo:
  freshness_minutes: 60
  availability_pct: 99.5        # loads succeeding per 30 days
  quality_pass_pct: 99.0        # rows passing fail+quarantine rules
rules:
  - id: orders_pk_unique
    dimension: uniqueness
    sql: "COUNT(*) = COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)"
    tier: fail
  - id: orders_amount_valid
    dimension: validity
    row_condition: "amount >= 0"
    tier: quarantine
    quarantine_table: prod.silver_sales.orders_quarantine
  - id: orders_email_null_rate
    dimension: completeness
    metric: "avg(CASE WHEN email IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)"
    threshold: {max: 0.02}
    tier: warn
monitors:
  volume: {method: weekday_zscore, window_days: 28, sd: 3}
  schema: {on_change: alert, on_key_drop: fail}
alert_route: "#sales-data-oncall"
runbook: docs/runbooks/orders.md
```

## Quarantine pattern (SQL)
```sql
INSERT INTO prod.silver_sales.orders_quarantine
SELECT *, 'amount_negative' AS dq_reason, current_timestamp() AS dq_at
FROM staged_orders WHERE NOT (amount >= 0);
MERGE INTO prod.silver_sales.orders t
USING (SELECT * FROM staged_orders WHERE amount >= 0) s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;
```

## Incident severity
| Sev | Definition | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Wrong or missing Tier 1 data visible to execs, customers, or regulators | Page on-call now; notify consumers within 1 hour; stop downstream publish |
| 2 | Tier 1 late beyond 2x SLO, or Tier 2 wrong | Fix same business day; status note to consumers |
| 3 | Tier 3 issue or warn-level drift | Ticket; fix in sprint |

## Runbook skeleton
1. Acknowledge and set severity. 2. Check lineage for upstream cause (source outage, schema change, late file). 3. Contain: pause downstream jobs, flag dashboards as stale. 4. Fix and backfill idempotently. 5. Verify rules pass and reconcile. 6. Notify consumers. 7. Blameless review within 5 business days; add a rule that would have caught it.

## Worked example
Revenue dashboard showed a 40% drop. Cause: source sent a partial file. A volume monitor (weekday z-score) would have fired at load; a Tier 1 reconciliation rule (gold revenue vs source total within 0.5%) set to fail would have blocked publish. Both were added and the incident runbook updated.

## Anti-patterns
- Dropping bad rows silently with no quarantine or count.
- Every rule set to fail, so pipelines stop for cosmetic issues and people disable checks.
- Alerts to an individual's email.
- Static volume thresholds that ignore weekday/seasonal patterns.
- Quality checks only in the consumption layer, after bad data has spread.

## Output
Criticality register, rule YAML per table, monitor config, SLOs in contracts, severity table, runbooks. Publish with publish-lakehouse-docs-to-repo; patterns go into design-engineering-patterns.

## Completion checks
- Every Tier 1 table has fail-tier uniqueness and reconciliation rules, freshness and volume monitors, and an SLO.
- Every quarantine table has a reason column and a review owner.
- Every alert has a team route and a runbook link.
- New rules start as warn unless they protect keys or Tier 1 reconciliation.

## Basis
- Lakeflow pipeline expectations: https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectations
- Databricks data profiling (formerly Lakehouse Monitoring): https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/data-quality-monitoring/data-profiling
- dbt test severity: https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/resource-configs/severity
- Snowflake data metric functions: https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/data-quality-intro
- Google SRE book, SLOs: https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/
- DAMA-DMBOK2 data quality dimensions (chapter 13), DAMA International.

skills.name: design-databricks-physical-model
skills.description: Translate a logical lakehouse model into Databricks Delta tables, views, types, constraints, and workload-appropriate layouts. Use for physical ERDs, draft DDL, surrogate implementations, Unity Catalog placement, and enforcement decisions.
skills.content:
---
name: design-databricks-physical-model
description: >-
  Translate a logical lakehouse model into Databricks Delta tables, views,
  types, constraints, and workload-appropriate layouts. Use for physical ERDs,
  draft DDL, surrogate implementations, Unity Catalog placement, and enforcement
  decisions.
---
# Design a Databricks physical model

## Inputs
Read the logical model, layer contracts, query workload, expected volumes, target Databricks Runtime/SQL capabilities, and existing repository/deployment conventions. Treat unverified capabilities as open dependencies.

## Procedure
1. Map entities to tables, views, materialized views, or nested structures with reasons. Record logical-to-physical mappings and any denormalization or subtype transformation.
2. Use existing catalog/schema/environment conventions. Keep object names stable across environments where practical, with environment selection handled by existing configuration. Do not invent deployed schemas or grants.
3. Define columns, precise types, decimal precision/scale, timestamp semantics, nullability, defaults, comments, keys, and provenance. Preserve identifiers whose leading zeros or nonnumeric characters carry meaning.
4. Document every constraint's enforcement. Databricks primary/foreign keys are informational; use explicit uniqueness and relationship checks. Use supported NOT NULL and CHECK constraints for applicable row rules. Do not enable optimizer trust such as RELY without validated invariants.
5. Evaluate surrogate generation against rebuilds, parallel writers, and target-engine restrictions. Verify identity-column compatibility instead of assuming it supports the intended writer topology.
6. Choose layout from workload and supported features. Evaluate liquid clustering or supported automatic clustering; do not combine liquid clustering with partitioning or ZORDER. Document required runtime/table features and maintenance ownership. Do not translate traditional B-tree indexing advice directly to Delta tables.
7. Specify views and access boundaries required by the model, including tenant and sensitive columns. A naming convention or tenant column alone does not enforce access isolation. Reuse the established security design.
8. Generate draft DDL and required data checks. Include compatibility notes, deployment ordering, and migration implications; producing a model does not authorize executing production DDL.

## Output
Produce a physical ERD, logical-to-physical mapping, draft DDL, constraint enforcement matrix, layout rationale, access requirements, and validation queries. Label SQL as executed, syntax-checked, or unexecuted.

## Completion checks
Verify types across joins, grain/key alignment, constraints versus actual guarantees, feature compatibility, and retained logical business meaning. Keep partition/layout choices evidence-based rather than mandatory for every table.

## Basis
DAMA-DMBOK2 chapter 5, printed pp. 148–150, 156–158, 161–162, adapted using https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/constraints and https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/clustering .

skills.name: design-dimensions-and-history
skills.description: Design a dimension and choose history behavior per attribute, including mixed Type 1 and Type 2 changes. Use for conformed dimensions, surrogate keys, current versus historical reporting, late changes, and dimension-version resolution in Databricks.
skills.content:
---
name: design-dimensions-and-history
description: >-
  Design a dimension and choose history behavior per attribute, including mixed
  Type 1 and Type 2 changes. Use for conformed dimensions, surrogate keys,
  current versus historical reporting, late changes, and dimension-version
  resolution in Databricks.
---
# Design dimensions and history

## Inputs
Read reporting requirements, business identity rules, source history/sequence evidence, existing conformed dimensions, and correction policies. Do not assign Type 2 merely because an attribute can change.

## Procedure
1. Declare the business entity grain and the row/version grain. Separate the durable business identity, source identifiers, and dimension-version surrogate key. Specify namespace and unknown/inferred member treatment.
2. For each attribute, ask whether old facts should retain the previous value, show the latest corrected value, or expose a limited prior value. Classify fixed/Type 0, overwrite/Type 1, versioned/Type 2, or limited-history/Type 3, with a business reason.
3. For mixed history, list the exact Type 2 change-detection attributes. Define whether a Type 1 correction updates every version of that business identity or only designated rows. Do not accidentally version technical ingestion metadata.
4. Define valid-time intervals as [effective_from, effective_to), with one explicit open-end convention. Separate source-effective time from recorded/processing time. If the source gives only observation time, label the resulting history accordingly.
5. Define fact lookup using the business key and event time within the interval; specify the behavior when zero or multiple versions match. Do not join every historical fact to the current dimension row by default.
6. Specify backdated changes, tied effective times, reactivation, deletes, and replay. A backdated change may split an existing interval and require fact-key repair. Preserve all changes required for history, including multiple versions within a batch.
7. Choose a stable surrogate strategy and document allocation, collision checks if hashed, rebuild behavior, and concurrency constraints. A hash of only the business key does not distinguish Type 2 versions.
8. Align shared attributes and definitions with other dimensions. Define role-playing use without duplicating a conformed dimension unnecessarily.

## Output
Produce a dimension specification, attribute-level SCD matrix, key design, interval/lookup rules, and before/after examples for an overwrite, version change, and late correction.

## Completion checks
Check unique version keys, the documented current-row invariant, non-overlapping intervals, correct boundary timestamps, deterministic replay, and stable fact attribution. A deleted identity may legitimately have no current row under the declared policy. Never claim a platform's SCD option implements the full business correction policy without checking its behavior.

## Basis
DAMA-DMBOK2 chapter 5, printed pp. 139–140, 142–143, and 157. Interval, hybrid-SCD, and fact-repair procedures extend the chapter's history concepts.

skills.description: Design and publish reusable lakehouse patterns and standards for developers and data engineers to follow, such as naming conventions, layer templates, ingestion, SCD, merge, quality-check, and folder/repo patterns. Use when the team needs a standard, when the same problem is solved inconsistently, or when onboarding engineers.

name: design-engineering-patterns
description: >-
  Design and publish reusable lakehouse patterns and standards for developers
  and data engineers to follow, such as naming conventions, layer templates,
  ingestion, SCD, merge, quality-check, and folder/repo patterns. Use when the
  team needs a standard, when the same problem is solved inconsistently, or when
  onboarding engineers.
---
# Design engineering patterns

## Inputs
Read existing conventions, repos, catalogs, and pipelines first; find what engineers already do and where it diverges. Read the platform (e.g. Databricks Unity Catalog), team size and skills, and governance or security rules. Adopt and tighten what exists before inventing new standards.

## Pattern catalog to consider
- **Naming conventions:** catalogs, schemas, tables, views, columns, keys, jobs/pipelines, notebooks, files, environments, and tags. Decide case (snake_case), singular vs plural, layer prefixes or schema-per-layer (bronze_/silver_/gold_ or bronze.*), fact_/dim_/bridge_ prefixes, key suffixes (_id, _sk, _bk), timestamp suffixes (_ts, _utc, _date), boolean prefixes (is_, has_), audit columns, reserved words, abbreviations list, and max lengths.
- **Layer templates:** standard Bronze envelope columns, Silver typed/deduped shape, Gold fact and dimension shapes.
- **Ingestion patterns:** batch file, incremental/CDC, streaming, API pulls; checkpointing, schema-drift and rejected-record handling.
- **Transformation patterns:** idempotent MERGE/upsert with ordering, SCD Type 1/2 template, late-arriving data, soft and hard deletes, backfill and replay.
- **Data quality patterns:** standard expectations (not null, unique, referential, range, freshness), quarantine tables, reason codes, alerting.
- **Code and repo patterns:** folder layout, parameterized environment config, reusable libraries, testing, code review checklist, CI/CD promotion.
- **Security and governance patterns:** grants by role, PII tagging and masking, row filters, ownership tags.
- **Documentation patterns:** table and column comments, data contract template, decision record template.

## Procedure
1. Pick the patterns that solve real, recurring problems for this team; prioritize naming and layer templates first, since everything else depends on them.
2. For each pattern write: problem it solves, when to use and when not to, the rule, a concrete good and bad example, a copy-paste template (SQL/Python/YAML) where useful, and how compliance is checked.
3. Keep rules few, unambiguous, and testable. Prefer conventions a linter or a SQL check against information_schema can enforce.
4. Make the naming convention a single reference table: object type, pattern, example, notes.
5. Show how the patterns fit together end to end with one worked example (a source landing in Bronze through a Gold fact), using Lucid or Mermaid for the flow diagram.
6. Define governance of the patterns: owner, versioning, how engineers propose changes, how exceptions are approved and recorded, and migration guidance for existing objects that don't comply.
7. Review with representative engineers before publishing; mark the standard draft until approved. Never claim team sign-off that wasn't given.

## Output
A pattern guide (or one page per pattern) with the naming reference table, templates, examples, compliance checks, and a change process, published where the team keeps docs.

## Completion checks
Every rule has an example and a way to verify it. Patterns don't contradict each other or the existing medallion and modeling skills. Existing nonconforming objects have a migration or grandfathering decision rather than being silently ignored.

skills.description: Design Gold fact tables with explicit grain, dimensions, measures, and aggregation rules. Use when modeling analytical events, periodic snapshots, accumulating snapshots, factless relationships, KPI inputs, or aggregates.
skills.content:
---
name: design-gold-facts-and-measures
description: >-
  Design Gold fact tables with explicit grain, dimensions, measures, and
  aggregation rules. Use when modeling analytical events, periodic snapshots,
  accumulating snapshots, factless relationships, KPI inputs, or aggregates.
---
# Design Gold facts and measures

## Inputs
Read the business questions, logical entities, detailed source/Silver grains, available history, and existing conformed dimensions and measures.

## Procedure
1. Select the business process and write a one-row grain sentence before listing measures or dimension keys. Identify a business occurrence key; dimension foreign keys alone need not identify an event uniquely.
2. Choose transaction/event, periodic snapshot, accumulating snapshot, or factless fact based on the process. Specify whether rows append, replace, or change with milestones. For snapshots, define population coverage and whether missing rows mean zero or no observation.
3. Check every measure against the declared grain. Record definition, units, event population, inclusion/exclusion rules, formula, null behavior, and time basis. Separate quantities at different grains into different facts.
4. Classify aggregation by each relevant dimension, especially time. Preserve numerators and denominators for rates and weighted averages. Do not sum distinct counts or average averages without a valid mathematical basis.
5. Select conformed dimensions and role-playing keys. Define event-time versus current-state attribution, unknown/inferred members, late-arriving dimension resolution, and repair behavior.
6. Model multiple agents, queues, institutions, reasons, or other multivalued relationships at their actual grain. Define counting and allocation policies before joining them to a fact. Never mask fan-out with DISTINCT without proving the business result.
7. Specify late facts, corrections, cancellations, deletion, reprocessing, and aggregate restatement. Reconcile atomic facts to source business events, accounting for explicit exclusions.
8. Answer representative questions using query sketches. For multiple facts, aggregate each to compatible conformed dimensions before joining unless a proven relationship supports another approach.

## Output
Produce a fact specification: process, grain, occurrence identity, fact type, dimensions, measure/additivity table, temporal attribution, load/correction behavior, and reconciliation rules. Include a bus-matrix row and example analytical queries.

## Completion checks
Demonstrate one-count-per-occurrence behavior, valid totals across joins, and expected handling of missing dimensions. Label Gold detail facts and aggregates separately; Gold does not imply pre-aggregation.

## Basis
DAMA-DMBOK2 chapter 5, printed pp. 138–140 and 147–150. Snapshot taxonomy, additivity checks, and incremental correction cases are analytical-design extensions.

skills.name: design-logical-entities-and-keys
skills.description: Design implementation-independent entities, attributes, domains, and identifiers. Use when resolving logical grain, candidate keys, normalization, reference codes, supertypes, or identity namespaces before Databricks physical design.
skills.content:
---
name: design-logical-entities-and-keys
description: >-
  Design implementation-independent entities, attributes, domains, and
  identifiers. Use when resolving logical grain, candidate keys, normalization,
  reference codes, supertypes, or identity namespaces before Databricks physical
  design.
---
# Design logical entities and keys

## Inputs
Read the conceptual model, requirements, source evidence, and existing naming/domain standards. Identify unapproved assumptions before using them as constraints.

## Procedure
1. State what one instance of every entity means, including its business scope and whether it represents an event, current state, or historical version.
2. Assign attributes by meaning and dependency. Define each attribute, its logical domain, optionality, units, and source. Do not substitute a platform data type for a business definition.
3. Identify minimal candidate keys, choose a logical identifier, and record alternate identities. Specify namespace, stability, nullability, reuse, and temporal uniqueness. A surrogate key does not eliminate duplicate business identities.
4. Test candidate keys against evidence. Never assume email, name plus birth date, or phone uniquely identifies a person. Keep source identity separate from any proposed mastered identity.
5. Examine functional dependencies. For relational designs, check repeating groups, partial dependencies, and transitive dependencies. Use higher normal forms only for demonstrated anomalies and validate lossless decomposition. Do not decompose a genuine ternary rule into unrelated pairs.
6. Resolve multivalued relationships through associative entities with their own grain and relationship attributes. Identify historical associations separately from current ones.
7. Define shared domains: code sets, ranges, formats, precision requirements, and cross-field rules. Scope shared codes by their domain to avoid collisions. Distinguish unknown, not applicable, and missing.
8. Document justified abstraction, retained redundancy, and the effect of any denormalization. Keep technology-specific storage choices for physical design.

## Output
Produce a logical ERD, entity/attribute dictionary, candidate and alternate key register, domain register, relationship rules, and a record of normalization or abstraction decisions. Include evidence and unresolved identity questions.

## Completion checks
Verify that attributes belong at the declared grain and every key has a uniqueness scope. Ensure a physical surrogate proposal preserves the logical uniqueness rule. Reuse approved definitions rather than creating synonymous entities.

## Basis
DAMA-DMBOK2 chapter 5, printed pp. 133–136, 146–147, and 150–156. Validate dependencies directly rather than treating abbreviated textbook examples as universal rules.

skills.name: design-semantic-layer-and-metrics
skills.description: Design a governed semantic layer so every tool computes metrics the same way: metric definition specs (formula, grain, filters, owner), certified vs exploratory metrics, metric views or semantic models, BI integration, and change control. Use when two reports disagree on a number, when a domain publishes KPIs, when adopting a semantic/metrics tool, or when AI/BI assistants need trusted definitions.
skills.content:
---
name: design-semantic-layer-and-metrics
description: >-
  Design a governed semantic layer so every tool computes metrics the same way:
  metric definition specs (formula, grain, filters, owner), certified vs
  exploratory metrics, metric views or semantic models, BI integration, and
  change control. Use when two reports disagree on a number, when a domain
  publishes KPIs, when adopting a semantic/metrics tool, or when AI/BI
  assistants need trusted definitions.
---
# Design the semantic layer and metrics

## Inputs
KPI list and current definitions (often spread across BI tools and spreadsheets), the consumption-layer model (facts and conformed dimensions from design-gold-facts-and-measures and design-dimensions-and-history, or equivalent marts), BI tools in use, metric owners, and the access model.

## Procedure
1. **Harvest current definitions** from dashboards, SQL, and spreadsheets. List every variant of the same KPI and where it is used.
2. **Resolve conflicts** with the business owner; record the decision and why. Use explain-tradeoffs-to-business when variants change reported numbers.
3. **Write a metric spec** per metric (template below). Required: name, business definition, formula, measure type, grain/time dimension, allowed dimensions, filters, owner, certification status.
4. **Classify measure type** because it decides how it rolls up: additive (sum across all dimensions, e.g. revenue), semi-additive (not across time, e.g. balances, inventory: use last/average over time), non-additive (ratios, distinct counts: compute from components, never sum or average a ratio).
5. **Choose the implementation** (decision table). Define metrics once, close to the data, and let tools query them.
6. **Certify.** Certified metrics need: spec complete, owner, tests (reconciliation to a known number), and documentation. Everything else is exploratory and labeled so.
7. **Integrate BI**: tools read certified metrics from the semantic layer; disallow re-defining certified metrics in workbook calculations for official dashboards.
8. **Control change** (rules below) through pull requests via publish-lakehouse-docs-to-repo.

## Implementation options
| Option | Fits when | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Databricks Unity Catalog metric views | Databricks-centered, want definitions governed in the catalog and usable in SQL, dashboards, Genie | Defined in YAML (spec 1.1); queried with `MEASURE()`; supports materialization |
| dbt Semantic Layer (MetricFlow) | dbt already the transformation standard, multiple warehouses/BI tools | Definitions live in the dbt repo |
| Snowflake semantic views | Snowflake-centered, Cortex Analyst or agent use | Schema-level object; `CREATE SEMANTIC VIEW` or Snowsight wizard |
| BI-native model (Power BI semantic model, Looker LookML, Tableau) | One dominant BI tool | Risk: definitions trapped in one tool |
| Plain curated views | Small scope, few metrics | No measure-aware aggregation; ratios break when re-aggregated |
Rule: if more than one consumer tool needs the metric, define it outside the BI tool.

## Metric spec YAML template
```yaml
metric: net_revenue
label: Net revenue
status: certified            # certified | exploratory | deprecated
owner: grp_finance_analytics
business_definition: >-
  Invoiced revenue after discounts and returns, excluding tax and shipping.
measure_type: additive
formula: "SUM(line_amount - discount_amount) - SUM(return_amount)"
source: prod.gold_sales.fact_order_line
time_dimension: invoice_date
grain: order_line
allowed_dimensions: [customer_segment, product_category, region, sales_channel]
filters: ["order_status <> 'cancelled'", "is_test_order = false"]
currency: reporting currency at daily rate (see fx policy)
tests:
  - reconcile_to: "GL account 4000 monthly total, tolerance 0.1%"
version: 2.0
changelog:
  - "2.0: returns now subtracted on return date, not order date (ADR-014)"
```

## Metric view template (Databricks, YAML spec version 1.1)
```yaml
version: 1.1
source: prod.gold_sales.fact_order_line
filter: order_status <> 'cancelled' AND is_test_order = false
fields:
  - name: invoice_month
    expr: date_trunc('MONTH', invoice_date)
  - name: region
    expr: region
measures:
  - name: net_revenue
    expr: SUM(line_amount - discount_amount) - SUM(return_amount)
  - name: order_count
    expr: COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)
  - name: avg_order_value
    expr: (SUM(line_amount - discount_amount) - SUM(return_amount)) / COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)
```
`fields` and the older `dimensions` keyword are equivalent; `fields` is the documented preferred term. Version 1.1 adds features such as joins with cardinality and parameters; check the feature availability table for the runtime each needs. Create with `CREATE VIEW prod.semantic.sales_metrics WITH METRICS LANGUAGE YAML AS $$ ... $$`.
Query: `SELECT invoice_month, region, MEASURE(net_revenue) FROM prod.semantic.sales_metrics GROUP BY ALL;`

## Change control rules
| Change | Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Description, label | Minor version; PR review by owner |
| New allowed dimension | Minor; check fan-out (bridge tables can double-count) |
| Formula or filter change that alters values | Major version; ADR; announce with before/after numbers; keep old as `_v1` deprecated for one reporting cycle |
| Retire | Mark deprecated, notify consumers from lineage, remove after agreed date |

## Worked example
Sales and Finance reported different "revenue" (gross vs net of returns). Resolution: two certified metrics, `gross_bookings` (Sales owner) and `net_revenue` (Finance owner), each with spec and tests; "revenue" alone banned as a metric name. Average order value defined as ratio of components so it re-aggregates correctly by region.

## Anti-patterns
- Averaging a ratio across groups (average of daily conversion rates).
- Summing semi-additive balances across months.
- Same name, different formulas in different tools.
- Certifying a metric with no owner or reconciliation test.
- Metrics joining through many-to-many bridges without de-duplication.

## Output
Metric catalog (specs), chosen implementation, semantic objects, certification list, BI integration rules, change-control process.

## Completion checks
- Every certified metric has owner, formula, measure type, grain, filters, and a passing reconciliation test.
- No ratio or distinct count is defined as a pre-aggregated column that tools re-sum.
- Official dashboards use only certified metrics.
- Major changes have an ADR and a deprecation window.

## Basis
- Unity Catalog metric views: https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/uc-semantics/metric-views
- Metric view YAML reference (spec 1.1, fields/dimensions): https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/uc-semantics/metric-views/yaml-reference
- CREATE VIEW ... WITH METRICS: https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-create-view
- dbt Semantic Layer / MetricFlow: https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/use-dbt-semantic-layer/dbt-sl
- Snowflake semantic views: https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/views-semantic/overview
- Kimball Group, additive/semi-additive/non-additive facts: https://www.kimballgroup.com/data-warehouse-business-intelligence-resources/kimball-techniques/dimensional-modeling-techniques/additive-semi-additive-non-additive-fact/

---
name: design-silver-canonical-model
description: >-
  Model validated Silver entities, events, and nested child collections from
  Bronze records. Use when choosing canonical grain, typed mappings,
  deduplication, update ordering, schema-drift handling, or current-state versus
  history structures.
---
# Design a Silver canonical model

## Inputs
Read the Bronze contract, logical model, profiled source behavior, layer responsibilities, and downstream history requirements. Use actual source paths and verified identity namespaces.

## Procedure
1. Declare each target grain as entity, event, child occurrence, relationship, or version. Preserve needed event detail and separate entities with different grains.
2. Map source paths to named, typed columns with domain rules, null handling, units, source time semantics, and provenance. Distinguish missing, explicit null, malformed, and out-of-domain values.
3. For every array, choose retain, flatten, or separate child table based on query and relationship needs. Specify a stable child identity when possible. An array position is not a stable cross-version key unless the source guarantees it. Do not explode independent arrays together and accidentally multiply rows.
4. Specify the business key and full source order: version/sequence, timestamp, and justified tie-breaker. Quarantine or flag conflicting equal-order records if the source gives no valid precedence. A hash can identify payload differences but cannot establish business recency.
5. Distinguish exact duplicate removal from version selection. For current-state upserts, compare incoming order with persisted target order so an older later batch cannot overwrite a newer record. Preserve deletes with enough sequence state to prevent stale resurrection.
6. Decide whether all versions, current state, or both are required. Do not collapse multiple history-bearing changes to the last row of a batch. State correction, late-arrival, null-update, delete, and replay behavior.
7. Define quality checks and a reason-coded exception path. Keep reusable business integration in Silver where justified; leave report-specific aggregation to Gold.

## Output
Produce a Silver model, typed source-to-target mapping, child-table designs, identity/order contract, current/history decision, quality rules, and transformation pseudocode. Include duplicate, stale update, tied sequence, late delete, and schema-change examples.

## Completion checks
Verify deterministic replay, cross-batch ordering, tenant-safe joins, and explicit row-count changes. Distinguish a stream checkpoint, event-time watermark, and business update sequence; none substitutes for the other.

## Basis
DAMA-DMBOK2 chapter 5, printed pp. 146, 148, 150–156, adapted to Silver. For an AUTO CDC implementation, verify the target runtime and current API at https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/developer/ldp-python-ref-apply-changes .

skills.name: design-streaming-and-latency-architecture
skills.description: Decide between batch, micro-batch, and continuous streaming based on how fresh data really needs to be, then design the stream correctly: watermarks, exactly-once and idempotency, late data, state, cost trade-offs, and failure recovery. Use when someone asks for "real-time", when designing CDC or event ingestion, or when a streaming job is costly or unreliable.
skills.content:
---
name: design-streaming-and-latency-architecture
description: >-
  Decide between batch, micro-batch, and continuous streaming based on how fresh
  data really needs to be, then design the stream correctly: watermarks,
  exactly-once and idempotency, late data, state, cost trade-offs, and failure
  recovery. Use when someone asks for "real-time", when designing CDC or event
  ingestion, or when a streaming job is costly or unreliable.
---
# Design streaming and latency architecture

## Inputs
Consumer decisions and how fast they act on data, source type (files, CDC, Kafka/Kinesis/Event Hubs, APIs), event volume and peaks, ordering and late-arrival behavior, target tables and merge keys, cost tolerance, and on-call capacity.

## Procedure
1. **Ask what decision the data drives and how fast someone acts.** A dashboard viewed each morning does not need seconds. Record the required freshness as an SLO.
2. **Pick a freshness tier** and processing mode (table and rules below).
3. **Choose the engine pattern.** Databricks default: Structured Streaming with Auto Loader for files or Kafka source, Delta sink, triggered with `availableNow` for scheduled incremental or `processingTime` for continuous micro-batch; Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines for managed streaming tables. Snowflake: Snowpipe / Snowpipe Streaming plus Dynamic Tables (target lag) or Streams and Tasks. Iceberg: Flink or Spark streaming writers; mind commit frequency and small files.
4. **Design event time handling**: event time column, watermark, late-data policy.
5. **Design for exactly-once end to end**: checkpointing + idempotent sink.
6. **Bound state** (aggregations, dedup, stream-stream joins) with watermarks and TTLs.
7. **Plan failure recovery and backfill** before go-live.
8. **Estimate cost** for always-on vs triggered (plan-cost-and-capacity) and explain the trade-off with explain-tradeoffs-to-business.

## Freshness tiers
| Tier | Freshness SLO | Mode | Typical uses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| T0 operational | < 10 s | Continuous streaming or an operational store, not the lakehouse | Fraud blocking, live routing |
| T1 near real-time | 10 s - 5 min | Continuous micro-batch (`processingTime`) | Ops dashboards, alerting |
| T2 frequent | 5 - 60 min | Scheduled incremental (`availableNow` every N min) | Intraday reporting |
| T3 daily/hourly | > 1 h | Batch incremental | Most analytics, finance |

## Decision rules
- Default to the slowest tier that meets the SLO; each tier faster costs more compute and on-call effort.
- Use incremental streaming APIs even for batch (`availableNow`): you get checkpoints and exactly-once without always-on cost.
- Go continuous only if the SLO is under ~5-15 minutes *and* someone acts within that window.
- Sub-second needs are an application/operational database problem; land the results in the lakehouse afterward.
- If the source only updates hourly, streaming cannot make it fresher.

## Watermarks and late data
Watermark = how long to wait for late events before finalizing a window. Set from measured lateness: p99 of `ingest_time - event_time` plus margin.
```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
agg = (spark.readStream.table("prod.bronze_iot.readings")
  .withWatermark("event_time", "30 minutes")
  .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "5 minutes"), "device_id")
  .agg(F.avg("temp").alias("avg_temp")))
(agg.writeStream
   .option("checkpointLocation", "/Volumes/prod/chk/iot_5min")
   .outputMode("append")
   .trigger(processingTime="1 minute")
   .toTable("prod.silver_iot.readings_5min"))
```
Late-data policy options: (a) drop after watermark and count drops; (b) route late rows to a side table and reprocess daily; (c) for financial facts, keep raw events and recompute affected windows in a nightly batch correction. Pick and document per table.

## Exactly-once and idempotency
- Spark/Delta: checkpoint + Delta transactional sink gives exactly-once for the stream. One checkpoint per query; never share or reuse checkpoints across queries.
- For `foreachBatch` MERGE, make it idempotent: dedupe within the batch on key + latest sequence, and merge on business key with a sequence/version guard.
```python
from pyspark.sql.window import Window
def upsert(batch_df, batch_id):
    latest = (batch_df.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(
        Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.col("seq").desc())))
        .filter("rn = 1").drop("rn"))
    latest.createOrReplaceTempView("s")
    batch_df.sparkSession.sql("""
      MERGE INTO prod.silver_sales.orders t USING s ON t.order_id = s.order_id
      WHEN MATCHED AND s.seq > t.seq THEN UPDATE SET *
      WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *""")
```
- For CDC, prefer the `AUTO CDC` APIs in Lakeflow pipelines (they replace `APPLY CHANGES` with the same syntax), which handle out-of-order sequencing and SCD1/SCD2.
- External sinks (APIs, Kafka) are at-least-once unless the sink deduplicates; include an idempotency key.

## State management
- Every stateful operation needs a watermark, or state grows forever.
- Dedup with `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark` (added in Spark 3.5.0) rather than unbounded `dropDuplicates`.
- Use the RocksDB state store for large state; monitor state rows and memory in the streaming query progress.
- Changing a stateful query's logic may require a new checkpoint and a backfill; plan it as a release.

## Failure recovery
| Failure | Recovery |
| --- | --- |
| Job crash | Restart from checkpoint (job retries with backoff) |
| Bad code wrote bad data | Delta time travel/`RESTORE` the table, fix, reset checkpoint, replay from source retention |
| Source retention shorter than outage | Backfill from Bronze/raw landing; this is why raw is kept |
| Schema change | Auto Loader schema evolution/rescued data column; alert per design-data-quality-and-observability |
Check source retention (e.g. Kafka topic retention) exceeds the longest outage you plan to survive.

## Cost trade-offs
Continuous runs 24x7 compute; scheduled `availableNow` every 15 minutes can cost a fraction for the same code. Present both with ranges based on measured runtime and current vendor prices. Never quote prices from memory.

## Worked example
"Real-time inventory dashboard." Store managers check it a few times a day; replenishment runs hourly. SLO set at 15 minutes (T2). Design: Auto Loader + `availableNow` job every 10 minutes, MERGE with sequence guard into Silver, metric view on top. Result: same code could switch to continuous later by changing the trigger.

## Anti-patterns
- "Real-time" with no SLO or decision attached.
- Stateful aggregations without watermarks.
- Sharing a checkpoint between two queries or deleting it casually.
- Non-idempotent `foreachBatch` (plain INSERT) causing duplicates on retry.
- Tiny commits every second to Iceberg/Delta without compaction.

## Output
Freshness SLO per table, chosen mode and trigger, watermark and late-data policy, idempotency design, state limits, recovery runbook, cost comparison.

## Completion checks
- Every stream has an SLO, checkpoint location, watermark (if stateful), and owner.
- MERGE sinks are idempotent under replay of the same batch.
- Source retention >= planned recovery window.
- Recovery has been tested by killing and restarting the job.

## Basis
- Structured Streaming production guidance: https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/structured-streaming/production
- Watermarks: https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/structured-streaming/watermarks
- Triggers / availableNow: https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/structured-streaming/triggers
- Lakeflow AUTO CDC APIs (replace APPLY CHANGES): https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/cdc
- Spark Structured Streaming guide: https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/streaming/index.html
- Snowflake Dynamic Tables: https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/dynamic-tables/overview

---
name: document-model-contracts-and-lineage
description: >-
  Produce an implementation-ready model dictionary, data contracts,
  source-to-target mappings, and requirement lineage. Use when handing a model
  to engineers, documenting a medallion product, or closing metadata gaps in an
  existing design.
---
# Document model contracts and lineage

## Inputs
Read the requirements, current conceptual/logical/physical artifacts, transformation design, source documentation, and existing contract format. Do not invent a new contract schema if an approved one exists.

## Procedure
1. Inventory model objects with stable identifiers and versions. Record each object's business purpose, grain, owner, layer, keys, history, quality promises, and intended consumers.
2. Document every target attribute with definition, source object/path, transformation, type/domain, units, null/default behavior, sensitivity, and temporal meaning. Label constants, generated keys, and derived measures explicitly.
3. Record joins, filters, deduplication, version selection, aggregation, and exception routing as part of mappings. A list of source column names is insufficient to reproduce an output.
4. Trace source → Bronze → Silver → Gold at table and column level where relevant, and requirement → conceptual concept → logical object → physical object separately. Include external reference data and calendar dependencies.
5. Define the consumer contract: schema, grain, identities, allowed values, freshness, history, late/corrected data behavior, deletion, and compatibility expectations. Name which rule is enforced where and what happens on failure.
6. Reconcile diagrams, dictionary, mappings, and DDL. Mark unavailable source fields and business decisions as gaps with owners rather than completing them with guesses.
7. Link rationale and rejected alternatives to decision records. Keep accessible business definitions alongside machine-readable contracts. Record approval status without implying review occurred.

## Output
Produce or update the model dictionary, source-to-target mapping, lineage view, consumer contract, and engineering handoff. Use existing repository locations; if absent, propose a consistent location before establishing one.

Minimum mapping columns: target object/attribute; definition; source object/path; expression or derivation; join/filter; data type/domain; null/default policy; history/time rule; quality check; requirement ID; evidence/status.

## Completion checks
Ensure every target field is traceable, every requirement has a supported model path or explicit gap, and every diagram agrees with its accompanying tables. Do not claim runtime lineage was observed when only design lineage was produced.

## Basis
DAMA-DMBOK2 chapter 5, printed pp. 125, 152–153, 159–160, and 163–164. Contract execution details extend the chapter's metadata and lineage requirements.

skills.name: explain-tradeoffs-to-business
skills.description: Use when a lakehouse design choice or trade-off needs business sign-off, funding, or explaining to leaders: turns it into a jargon-free one-page decision brief with simple diagrams showing reasoning, cost, time, risk, and impact.
skills.content:
---
name: explain-tradeoffs-to-business
description: >-
  Use when a lakehouse design choice or trade-off needs business sign-off,
  funding, or explaining to leaders: turns it into a jargon-free one-page
  decision brief with simple diagrams showing reasoning, cost, time, risk, and
  impact.
---
# Explain trade-offs to business leaders

## Inputs
Read the decision or ADR, the options considered, known costs and effort, risks, deadlines, and affected teams. Identify the audience: their role, what they care about (revenue, cost, risk, compliance, speed), how much time they have, and what you need from them (approve, fund, choose, or just be informed).

## Procedure
1. **Lead with the decision and business impact (BLUF / Minto).** First sentence: what we recommend or decided, and what it means for the business. Put the detail below it, never before it.
2. **Frame with SCQA.** Situation (facts they already accept), Complication (what changed), Question (usually "what should we do?"), Answer (the recommendation). If they would dispute the situation, fix that first.
3. **Present 2-4 real options**, including "do nothing." For each, cover cost, time to value, risk, and what the business gets or gives up. Make them truly distinct, not straw men.
4. **State reversibility.** Call each choice a one-way door (costly or impossible to undo, so decide carefully with wide input) or a two-way door (easy to reverse, so decide fast and set a review date). Match how much analysis you do to the door type.
5. **Quantify honestly.** Use ranges ("$40-60K a year"), not false precision. Label every number as measured, quoted, estimated, or assumed, and say where it came from. **Never invent numbers.** If a figure is unknown, write "unknown, need X to estimate" and say what it would take to find out.
6. **Translate the jargon** with the guide below. Remove acronyms or define them in plain words the first time. Use one analogy when it really helps, and say where it stops being accurate.
7. **Pick one diagram per idea** from the table below. Each diagram gets a title that states its takeaway ("Option B halves report delay"). Build diagrams in Lucid and attach or link them. Keep each one to about 7 elements.
8. **Tailor to the audience.** Executives get one page with a single ask. Business owners get impact on their process and their people. Finance gets total cost over 3 years. Risk and compliance get controls and remaining risk. Longer formats (Amazon-style 6-pager or PR/FAQ) are for big one-way doors that need group review.
9. **Keep the technical record linked.** The brief points to the ADR. It does not replace it. Note any decision made in the meeting back in the ADR.

## Concept-to-diagram guide
| To show | Use | Avoid when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What the system is and who uses it | Box-and-arrow context diagram (C4 level 1) | They need internals |
| How data moves between teams or steps | Data flow / swimlane | More than ~6 lanes |
| Layers or separation of duties | Layered (stacked) diagram | Flow order matters more |
| Choice that depends on conditions | Decision tree | More than 3 levels deep |
| Prioritizing many items on 2 factors | 2x2 matrix (e.g., value vs effort) | Factors aren't independent |
| Comparing options on several criteria | Options table with green/amber/red ratings plus a short reason | Colour alone carries the meaning |
| Cost over time / total cost | Total-cost or cost/benefit bar chart | Numbers are not sourced |
| Sequence, phases, milestones | Timeline / roadmap | Dates are guesses (use Now/Next/Later) |
| Likelihood vs impact of risks | Risk heat map | Fewer than 3 risks |
| What changes for users | Before/after diagram | The change isn't visible to them |
| Where volume or money flows and splits | Sankey | Few flows |
| Which assumption swings the outcome most | Tornado chart | No sensitivity data |
| How a total builds up or erodes | Waterfall chart | Parts don't add up |
| Build vs buy, commodity vs differentiator | Wardley map | Audience is new to maps (use a 2x2) |

## Jargon translation guide
| Term | Plain language |
| --- | --- |
| Medallion (Bronze/Silver/Gold) | Raw copy, cleaned and joined data, ready-to-use business data |
| SCD Type 2 | We keep the history of changes, e.g., a customer's old address for past orders |
| CDC | We copy only what changed, not everything every night |
| Data Vault | A storage design that tracks every source and change, built for audits and many changing systems, at the cost of more upkeep |
| Data contract | A written agreement on what data a team delivers, its format and freshness |
| Lineage | We can trace any report number back to its source |
| Schema evolution | Sources can add fields without breaking reports |
| Latency / SLA | How fresh the data is, and what we promise |
| Partitioning / clustering | Organizing data so queries run faster and cost less |
| Technical debt | Shortcuts we will pay for later in time and outages |

## Output template: one-page decision brief
```
Title: <decision as a claim>
Ask: <approve / choose / fund / FYI> by <date>
Bottom line: <recommendation + business impact in 2 sentences>
Situation / Complication: <2-3 lines>
Options:
| Option | Cost (range, source) | Time | Risk | Business gets | Business gives up | Door |
Recommendation and why: <3 reasons max>
What it costs if we wait: <impact>
Key assumptions and unknowns: <labelled estimates>
Diagram: <one Lucid visual with a takeaway title>
Next steps and owner: <...>   Technical detail: <ADR link>
```

## Completion checks
The first sentence states the decision and its impact. Every option shows cost, time, risk, gains, and give-ups. Every number is sourced or labelled as an estimate, and none is invented. Reversibility is stated. No unexplained acronyms. One idea per diagram, each with a takeaway title. The ask and the deadline are explicit. The brief links back to the ADR.

## Basis
- Minto Pyramid / SCQA: https://thebastrategytoolkit.com/frameworks/pyramid-principle/
- One-way vs two-way doors (Amazon 2015/2016 shareholder letters): https://blog.kindel.com/2019/06/27/one-way-and-two-way-doors/
- Amazon 6-pager and PR/FAQ: https://workingbackwards.com/resources/
- C4 model context diagrams: https://c4model.com/
- Wardley maps: https://learnwardleymapping.com/
- ADRs: https://adr.github.io/
- Diagram and chart selection: https://www.storytellingwithdata.com/ ; https://www.data-to-viz.com/

# Getting started

I'm a lakehouse architect: I take a data request from requirements through conceptual, logical, and physical data models, fit them to your lakehouse layering approach (medallion Bronze/Silver/Gold, Data Vault, Kimball-style marts, data mesh products, or your own), set engineering patterns, draw diagrams in Lucid, and publish ADRs, data contracts, and docs to GitHub for data engineers.
