1. What should I call you, and what do you want to call me?
2. Offer to connect Lucid so I can create model design diagrams; if they agree, start its connect flow.
3. Offer to connect GitHub, and ask which repo and base branch should hold ADRs, contracts, and lakehouse docs.
4. What platform is your lakehouse on (Databricks, or something else), which layering approach do you use or want (medallion, Data Vault, Kimball marts, data mesh, other), and do you have existing catalog, schema, or naming conventions I should follow?
5. Which subject area or data product do you want to start with?

Save the answers as memories, then start on their first subject area with scope-modeling-requirements.

skills.name: maintain-model-and-assess-change
skills.description: Assess a proposed model change and keep conceptual, logical, physical, and deployed designs aligned. Use for schema evolution, drift, changed business definitions, new source versions, dimension-history changes, or downstream impact analysis.
skills.content:
---
name: maintain-model-and-assess-change
description: >-
  Assess a proposed model change and keep conceptual, logical, physical, and
  deployed designs aligned. Use for schema evolution, drift, changed business
  definitions, new source versions, dimension-history changes, or downstream
  impact analysis.
---
# Maintain the model and assess change

## Inputs
Read the current and proposed versions, reason for change, source/deployed metadata available, requirement links, consumer contracts, lineage, and repository change process.

## Procedure
1. Identify the changed meaning, structure, grain, key, domain, relationship, time rule, quality promise, or access boundary. Separate a documentation correction from a real data-behavior change.
2. Trace impact through conceptual concepts, logical entities, physical objects, transformations, checks, facts/dimensions, aggregates, and consumer queries. Distinguish semantic compatibility from SQL/schema compatibility.
3. Classify consumers affected and whether history must be restated. Adding a nullable column may still break positional loads or SELECT * consumers; changing a key or SCD rule can require fact-key repair.
4. Plan evolution, backfill/rebuild, coexistence or compatibility views where needed, reconciliation, and rollback or forward repair. Verify that retained source history can support the proposed reconstruction.
5. Update the relevant models, definitions, mappings, contracts, decisions, and validation specifications together. Preserve the source and rationale of each rule change.
6. Compare deployed schema/behavior with the intended physical model using available read-only evidence. If live metadata is unavailable, state that drift assessment is limited to supplied artifacts. Do not automatically redefine the intended model to match unexplained drift.
7. Record why, what/how, who, where, model-change date, approval date/status, and implementation status separately. Follow existing version-control and review conventions without fabricating approvals or deployments.

## Output
Produce a change impact report, changed model artifacts, dependency list, compatibility classification, migration/backfill outline, validation plan, and decision/change record.

## Completion checks
Ensure related model levels remain consistent, affected consumers and history are accounted for, and recovery assumptions are explicit. Mark migrations as proposed unless executed within the authorized task. Distinguish model version from deployment version.

## Basis
DAMA-DMBOK2 chapter 5, printed pp. 159 and 163–164: maintenance, review, versioning, and change traceability.

skills.name: model-bridges-and-hierarchies
skills.description: Model many-to-many, ternary, recursive, and changing relationships without double-counting. Use for customer-to-institution offerings, agent assignments, multivalued contact reasons, organization hierarchies, or fact allocation through bridges.
skills.content:
---
name: model-bridges-and-hierarchies
description: >-
  Model many-to-many, ternary, recursive, and changing relationships without
  double-counting. Use for customer-to-institution offerings, agent assignments,
  multivalued contact reasons, organization hierarchies, or fact allocation
  through bridges.
---
# Model bridges and hierarchies

## Inputs
Read relationship business rules, participant identities, time semantics, source evidence, and the analytical questions that will traverse the association.

## Procedure
1. State the relationship as a business sentence and specify cardinality in both directions at a defined time. Distinguish an enduring association, a historical assignment, and a measurable event.
2. For a many-to-many relationship, create an associative entity or bridge with a declared grain and uniqueness rule. Put role, priority, effective dates, and other relationship-specific attributes on the association.
3. Preserve n-ary constraints. If an offering is provided by an institution, determine whether the customer relates to that institution-offering combination rather than to independent institution and offering lists.
4. For historical associations, define intervals, overlapping-assignment rules, and event-time joins. State whether the association references durable identities or dimension versions, and how version changes affect the relationship.
5. For hierarchy or network structures, define allowed parent counts, roots, orphan handling, cycle rules, and effective dates. Choose adjacency, closure, or a flattened analytical hierarchy according to traversal and reporting needs. Specify path uniqueness when multiple routes exist.
6. Define counting semantics: relationship count, distinct entity count, primary assignment, or weighted allocation. Use weights only with an approved allocation meaning, denominator, and applicable sum-to-one rule. Do not assume equal splitting is correct.
7. Provide query examples that show join multiplicity. Compare totals before and after traversal and explain any intentional change. Account for overlapping histories and missing parents.

## Output
Produce a relationship diagram, bridge/hierarchy specification, keys, time rules, supported traversal patterns, and anti-double-counting examples. Include rejected simpler models when they would lose a business rule.

## Completion checks
Verify no accidental Cartesian combinations, no duplicate relationship instances, and no unexplained measure inflation. Check cycles and temporal overlaps only against the declared business constraints; multiple parents are valid in a network.

## Basis
DAMA-DMBOK2 chapter 5, printed pp. 130–134, 151–156, and 160. Analytical allocation and historical bridge behavior extend the associative-entity patterns.

skills.name: model-calendar-and-local-time
skills.description: Design event timestamps, calendar and time dimensions, and institution-local reporting dates. Use when facts need UTC and local views, multiple time zones, fiscal calendars, daylight-saving handling, or time-zone assignment history.
skills.content:
---
name: model-calendar-and-local-time
description: >-
  Design event timestamps, calendar and time dimensions, and institution-local
  reporting dates. Use when facts need UTC and local views, multiple time zones,
  fiscal calendars, daylight-saving handling, or time-zone assignment history.
---
# Model calendar and local time

## Inputs
Read source timestamp definitions, business reporting boundaries, institutional calendar rules, and the required attribution of each fact to an institution or reporting location.

## Procedure
1. Distinguish event, source-update, effective, ingestion, and reporting times. Record original precision and source offset/zone information. Preserve a canonical UTC instant for actual events where the source supports one.
2. Choose timestamp storage and conversion behavior explicitly. Verify Databricks timestamp types, session time-zone behavior, and conversion functions against the target runtime before generating SQL. A local wall-clock timestamp without zone/offset may be ambiguous or invalid around daylight-saving transitions.
3. Store IANA region identifiers such as America/New_York when geographic time-zone rules are required. Do not treat a fixed UTC offset or ambiguous abbreviation as a substitute for historical zone rules.
4. Model institution-to-time-zone assignment at its actual grain. Use one attribute if one stable assignment is sufficient; use an effective-dated relationship when requirements support historical changes or multiple reporting locations. Define precedence for multiple valid choices.
5. Derive local date and time from the UTC instant using the applicable zone assignment. For a fact associated with multiple institutions, define a reporting association or view at fact-by-institution grain; do not duplicate the base fact without declaring the changed grain.
6. Define date and time dimension grains, role-playing keys, fiscal-calendar ownership, week boundaries, holidays, and unknown values. A generic time-of-day dimension describes clock labels, not unique instants; repeated local times require UTC/offset context.
7. Specify whether reporting restates when calendar or zone assignments change. Keep elapsed-duration calculations based on instants rather than subtracting local clock labels.

## Output
Produce a temporal contract, calendar/time dimensions when justified, assignment model, fact-key derivation rules, and examples around local midnight and both daylight-saving transitions. Identify timestamps whose source meaning remains unresolved.

## Completion checks
Check repeated and nonexistent local times, non-whole-hour offsets, date rollover, and temporal assignment uniqueness. Never invent fiscal or institutional calendar rules.

## Basis
Extend the time, domain, conformance, and history concepts in DAMA-DMBOK2 chapter 5, printed pp. 128, 135–136, 140, and 142–143. Consult https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/data-types/timestamp-type and https://www.iana.org/time-zones for implementation details.

skills.name: plan-migration-from-legacy-warehouse
skills.description: Plan and run a migration from a legacy warehouse or ETL stack (Teradata, Oracle, SQL Server, Netezza, Hadoop, older Snowflake/Redshift) to the lakehouse: inventory, complexity scoring, wave planning, code translation, parallel run, reconciliation, cutover and rollback, and decommission. Use when scoping, estimating, or executing a migration, or when a wave is ready to cut over.
skills.content:
---
name: plan-migration-from-legacy-warehouse
description: >-
  Plan and run a migration from a legacy warehouse or ETL stack (Teradata,
  Oracle, SQL Server, Netezza, Hadoop, older Snowflake/Redshift) to the
  lakehouse: inventory, complexity scoring, wave planning, code translation,
  parallel run, reconciliation, cutover and rollback, and decommission. Use when
  scoping, estimating, or executing a migration, or when a wave is ready to cut
  over.
---
# Plan a migration from a legacy warehouse

## Inputs
Legacy object catalog (tables, views, procedures, ETL jobs, schedules), query and usage logs (who queries what, how often), BI reports and their sources, data volumes, downstream feeds and extracts, license/contract end dates, target modeling scheme (select-modeling-scheme) and layering approach, and naming standards (design-engineering-patterns).

## Procedure
1. **Inventory everything** into the template below from system catalogs and query logs (e.g. Teradata DBQL, Oracle AWR/`DBA_` views, SQL Server DMVs, Snowflake `ACCESS_HISTORY`). Include consumers: reports, extracts, APIs.
2. **Prune.** Mark objects not queried in 90+ days as retire candidates; confirm with owners. Typically a meaningful share of legacy objects are unused, so measure rather than assume.
3. **Score complexity** (rubric below) and pick a strategy per object: lift-and-shift, re-platform (translate, keep model), or re-model.
4. **Plan waves** by business domain, so a domain's reports switch together. Wave 0 is a pilot: one domain, moderate complexity, a willing business owner.
5. **Land data first**: bulk historical load plus ongoing CDC/incremental feed so both systems stay in sync during parallel run.
6. **Translate code** with an automated converter where available (e.g. Databricks Lakebridge, which provides assessment, a transpiler, and a reconciler; SnowConvert for Snowflake targets), then review by hand: procedural loops, cursors, temp tables, MERGE semantics, date/NULL/collation differences.
7. **Parallel run** each wave for at least 2 full business cycles that include a month-end (often 4-8 weeks).
8. **Reconcile** daily with the queries below; publish a pass/fail dashboard.
9. **Cut over** with the checklist; keep rollback ready.
10. **Decommission** after the hold period: freeze legacy writes, archive, revoke, remove jobs, end licenses.

## Inventory template
| Object | Type | Domain | Size | Last used | Queries/30d | Consumers | Complexity score | Strategy | Wave | Owner | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

## Complexity rubric (score 1-3 each, total 5-15)
| Factor | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Code | Plain SQL view/select | Multi-step SQL, MERGE | Procedural (cursors, dynamic SQL, BTEQ/PLSQL logic) |
| Dependencies | 0-2 upstream | 3-10 | > 10 or circular |
| Consumers | 1-2 internal | Several reports | External/regulatory feeds |
| Data | < 100 GB, no history rules | History/SCD | Complex temporal or bitemporal |
| Platform features | Standard | Vendor functions | Vendor-specific (QUALIFY variants, macros, UDFs in C) |
5-7 = low (lift and translate), 8-11 = medium, 12-15 = high (consider re-model; budget extra testing).

## Reconciliation queries
Run the same query on both systems and compare results in a reconciliation table.
```sql
-- 1. Row counts by business date
SELECT order_date, COUNT(*) AS n FROM sales.orders
WHERE order_date BETWEEN :start AND :end GROUP BY order_date;

-- 2. Aggregates on measures and keys
SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) AS amt, SUM(quantity) AS qty,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers
FROM sales.orders GROUP BY order_date;

-- 3. Row-level hash diff (target side, after landing a legacy extract)
WITH l AS (SELECT order_id, md5(concat_ws('|', coalesce(cast(amount AS STRING),''),
            coalesce(status,''), cast(order_date AS STRING))) h FROM legacy_extract.orders),
     n AS (SELECT order_id, md5(concat_ws('|', coalesce(cast(amount AS STRING),''),
            coalesce(status,''), cast(order_date AS STRING))) h FROM prod.gold_sales.orders)
SELECT coalesce(l.order_id, n.order_id) AS order_id,
       CASE WHEN l.order_id IS NULL THEN 'missing_in_legacy'
            WHEN n.order_id IS NULL THEN 'missing_in_new'
            ELSE 'value_diff' END AS diff_type
FROM l FULL OUTER JOIN n ON l.order_id = n.order_id
WHERE l.h IS DISTINCT FROM n.h;
```
Normalize before hashing: trim strings, consistent decimal scale, timestamps in UTC, NULL as empty token. Hash diffs are for tables up to the size you can extract; for very large tables hash per partition/day, then drill down only into mismatched days.

**Tolerances:** counts and keys exact; sums of money exact to the cent unless a documented rounding change; floats within a stated relative tolerance (e.g. 1e-6). Every accepted difference is written down with a reason (bug fixed in new system, timezone correction).

## Cutover checklist
- [ ] Reconciliation green for N consecutive days including a month-end.
- [ ] Reports repointed and signed off by business owner.
- [ ] Downstream extracts/APIs repointed and consumers confirmed.
- [ ] Access model in place (design-security-and-access-model).
- [ ] Monitors and SLOs live (design-data-quality-and-observability).
- [ ] Rollback plan tested: legacy loads still running, report connections can be switched back within a stated window (e.g. 1 business day).
- [ ] Communication sent with date, impact, and support contact.
- [ ] Go/no-go meeting recorded as an ADR via publish-lakehouse-docs-to-repo.

## Rollback rules
Keep legacy loading in parallel through a hold period (commonly one month-end after cutover). Roll back if a Sev 1 data issue cannot be fixed within the agreed window or reconciliation breaks on a Tier 1 report. Decide the trigger before cutover, not during the incident.

## Decommission steps
Freeze legacy writes, take a final archive (export to object storage in Parquet with a manifest), revoke user access, disable jobs, keep read-only for audit if required, then end license and hardware. Track savings as measured (plan-cost-and-capacity).

## Worked example
120 legacy objects for finance. 35 unused in 90 days -> retired after owner sign-off. Scores: 50 low, 25 medium, 10 high. Wave 0: AP subledger (12 objects). Waves 1-3 by domain. High-score GL allocation procedure re-modeled into set-based SQL. Parallel run 6 weeks across a quarter close; hash diff found a timezone shift on posting timestamps, fixed and documented.

## Anti-patterns
- Migrating everything including dead objects.
- Translating procedural code line by line instead of set-based.
- Cutover without a month-end in the parallel run.
- Reconciling only row counts.
- Turning off legacy the day after cutover (no rollback).
- Changing the model and the platform in the same wave for high-risk reports without extra testing time.

## Output
Inventory with scores and strategy, wave plan, translation approach, reconciliation suite and dashboard, cutover and rollback runbook, decommission plan. Use explain-tradeoffs-to-business for wave sequencing and cutover go/no-go with leaders.

## Completion checks
- Every legacy object has a strategy (retire, lift, re-platform, re-model) and an owner.
- Every wave has reconciliation queries for counts, sums, and keys.
- Rollback trigger and window are written before cutover.
- Legacy decommission date and license end are tracked.

## Basis
- Databricks migration guide: https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/migration
- Databricks Lakebridge: https://databrickslabs.github.io/lakebridge/
- Snowflake SnowConvert: https://docs.snowflake.com/en/migrations/snowconvert-docs/general/about
- AWS Schema Conversion Tool: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/SchemaConversionTool/latest/userguide/CHAP_Welcome.html
- Martin Fowler, Strangler Fig pattern: https://martinfowler.com/bliki/StranglerFigApplication.html

skills.description: Profile source data and reconstruct an evidence-backed as-is model from schemas, DDL, JSON, SQL, and sample records. Use before modeling an unfamiliar source or when existing Databricks tables and documentation disagree.
skills.content:
---
name: profile-source-and-reverse-model
description: >-
  Profile source data and reconstruct an evidence-backed as-is model from
  schemas, DDL, JSON, SQL, and sample records. Use before modeling an unfamiliar
  source or when existing Databricks tables and documentation disagree.
---
# Profile sources and reverse-model

## Inputs
Read the supplied schemas, source contracts, existing transformations, table metadata, sample scope, and business questions. Use read-only access already available; if access is missing, prepare profiling queries and mark them unexecuted.

## Procedure
1. Inventory datasets with source/version, extraction time, covered period, row count when known, and whether each is an event feed, mutable snapshot, periodic snapshot, or reference dataset.
2. Reconstruct physical objects first. Capture columns or JSON paths, observed types, arrays, nullability, declared keys, joins in existing code, and update/delete signals. Separate observed storage from inferred business meaning.
3. Test candidate row identities within their proposed namespace. Measure null keys, duplicate keys, exact duplicate records, and multiple versions. Do not infer uniqueness from a small sample or a field name.
4. Profile value distributions, domain violations, parse failures, timestamp precision, late arrivals, sequence ties, identifier reuse, and schema drift. Distinguish absent JSON properties, explicit nulls, empty strings, and empty arrays.
5. Test proposed relationships with unmatched-key counts, multiplicity distributions, and join fan-out. Treat a relationship found in code as a hypothesis until verified. Include tenant boundaries in the checks where applicable.
6. Derive a logical interpretation and conceptual summary from the evidence. Record disagreements between source behavior, documentation, and business requirements instead of silently choosing one.

## Output
Produce a source evidence report with dataset inventory, as-is physical model, candidate identities, relationship evidence, anomalies, and open questions. Include query text and results when executed; otherwise provide a query plan. Label sample-limited findings with sample size, period, and limitations.

## Completion checks
Separate declared, observed, and inferred constraints. Show the grain implied by each source, not just its column list. Never report a query as passed when it was not run. Never expose personal sample values when aggregates or synthetic examples suffice.

## Basis
DAMA-DMBOK2 chapter 5, printed pp. 158–160: reverse engineering, profiling, metadata, and reusable patterns.

skills.description: Publish lakehouse design artifacts (ADRs, data contracts, model dictionaries, source-to-target mappings, naming and pattern standards, diagrams) to a GitHub repo on a new branch with a pull request. Use when a design is ready to hand to data engineers.

---
name: publish-lakehouse-docs-to-repo
description: >-
  Publish lakehouse design artifacts (ADRs, data contracts, model dictionaries,
  source-to-target mappings, naming and pattern standards, diagrams) to a GitHub
  repo on a new branch with a pull request. Use when a design is ready to hand
  to data engineers.
---
# Publish lakehouse docs to a repo

## Inputs
The target repo and base branch, the repo's existing docs layout and templates, and the finished artifacts from the modeling and pattern skills. Confirm the repo with the owner if it isn't already recorded in memory.

## Procedure
1. Inspect the repo first: existing docs folders, ADR numbering and template, contract format (YAML/JSON schema), naming conventions, CODEOWNERS, and PR template. Follow what exists; only propose a layout if none exists, e.g. `docs/adr/`, `docs/contracts/<domain>/`, `docs/models/<domain>/`, `docs/standards/`, `docs/diagrams/`.
2. Create a branch from the base branch named by the repo's convention, otherwise `docs/<domain>-<short-topic>`. Never commit directly to main or a protected branch.
3. Write the artifacts:
   - **ADRs:** one per significant decision, numbered sequentially, with title, status (Proposed), context, decision, alternatives considered, consequences, and links to requirements.
   - **Data contracts:** one per consumer-facing product with schema, grain, keys, allowed values, freshness, history, late/corrected data, deletion, quality checks, owner, and version.
   - **Model docs:** dictionary, source-to-target mapping, lineage, and draft DDL labeled unexecuted.
   - **Standards:** naming conventions and engineering patterns.
   - **Diagrams:** exported images or links to Lucid documents, plus Mermaid source where useful.
4. Keep each commit focused with a clear message. Never commit secrets, credentials, real personal data, or sample PII.
5. Open a pull request describing what was added, the decisions needing review, open questions, and suggested reviewers. Leave it for human review; never merge or approve it yourself, and never mark an ADR Accepted without recorded approval.
6. Report the branch, PR link, and the list of files added back to the owner.

## Completion checks
Every artifact sits in the agreed location and follows existing templates. ADR numbers don't collide. Contracts agree with the model docs and DDL. The PR is open, unmerged, and links to the decisions awaiting review.

skills.name: review-data-model-quality
skills.description: Review a conceptual, logical, or physical model against requirements, data evidence, and Databricks constraints. Use for design reviews, modeling PRs, grain/key validation, and identifying defects before engineering handoff.
skills.content:
---
name: review-data-model-quality
description: >-
  Review a conceptual, logical, or physical model against requirements, data
  evidence, and Databricks constraints. Use for design reviews, modeling PRs,
  grain/key validation, and identifying defects before engineering handoff.
---
# Review model quality

## Inputs
Read the model version, requirements, decisions, source evidence, relevant standards, and test results. Identify missing review inputs before scoring. Review the declared scheme and detail level, not an imagined broader design.

## Procedure
1. Walk each representative business question through the model. Flag unmet requirements and speculative structures that expand scope.
2. Check entity definitions, grain, candidate/alternate keys, cardinalities, attribute dependencies, domains, and naming. Reconcile diagrams with dictionaries and DDL.
3. Exercise duplicates, reused identifiers, tenant collisions, join fan-out, stale updates, sequence ties, deletes, missing dimensions, interval boundaries, and historical corrections where applicable. Identify actual counterexamples rather than general preferences.
4. Check layer responsibilities, retained history, model lineage, Databricks enforcement limits, feature prerequisites, access boundaries, and the cost/benefit of redundancy.
5. Record each finding with severity, affected object, violated rule or requirement, evidence, impact, proposed correction, and verification method. Distinguish defects, unresolved business decisions, and optional improvements.
6. Assess the chapter-based categories below. Supply evidence and remediation for each score. Use not-assessed when evidence is missing; do not convert absence of evidence into a pass or silently reweight the rubric.

| Category, paraphrased from the chapter | Maximum |
| --- | ---: |
| Requirements represented | 15 |
| Scope and metadata completeness | 15 |
| Appropriate scheme and detail level | 10 |
| Structural correctness | 15 |
| Appropriate reusable abstractions | 10 |
| Naming consistency | 5 |
| Diagram readability | 5 |
| Definition quality | 10 |
| Enterprise alignment | 5 |
| Agreement between metadata and actual data | 10 |

## Output
Produce a review report with model version, review scope, evidence inventory, prioritized findings, scorecard, unresolved questions, and disposition. Report a complete score out of 100 only when every category is assessable; otherwise report the assessed subtotal, assessed maximum, and missing categories.

## Completion checks
Do not invent a chapter-mandated pass threshold. Apply an existing organizational gate if supplied. An arbitrary high total never overrides a material grain, identity, history, or access defect. Keep human business approval distinct from the agent's technical recommendation. Label all unexecuted checks.

## Basis
DAMA-DMBOK2 chapter 5, printed pp. 158 and 161–166. Category weights follow Table 11 on printed p. 164; wording is paraphrased. Additional lakehouse checks are project-specific extensions.

skills.description: Turn a lakehouse modeling request into bounded, testable data requirements. Use when starting a subject area, clarifying reporting questions, or identifying missing grain, history, identity, and ownership requirements before designing tables.

description: >-
  Turn a lakehouse modeling request into bounded, testable data requirements.
  Use when starting a subject area, clarifying reporting questions, or
  identifying missing grain, history, identity, and ownership requirements
  before designing tables.
---
# Scope modeling requirements

## Inputs
Read the request, relevant project instructions, existing glossary, related models, and available source documentation. Work with available evidence; distinguish supplied facts, observed facts, proposals, and unresolved questions.

## Procedure
1. Identify the business process, users, decisions, required outputs, scope, exclusions, and freshness needs. Capture representative questions with expected answers or example rows.
2. Assign stable requirement IDs. Separate business meaning from source-system behavior and implementation preferences.
3. For each question, capture the thing being counted or measured, required detail, dimensions of analysis, history horizon, and whether results must reflect current knowledge or the state at event time.
4. Identify identity boundaries: tenant, source system, source instance, institution, customer, and service offering where relevant. Do not assume these are interchangeable or share one identifier.
5. Identify event, effective, and ingestion times; correction, deletion, retention, privacy, and access requirements. Record only requirements relevant to the requested product.
6. Look for reusable enterprise definitions and conformed structures. Preserve local terminology as aliases when reconciling it with approved enterprise terms.
7. Record modeling choices that remain open, the consequence of each, and the owner able to resolve them. Ask only questions that materially change the design; continue independent work with clearly labeled assumptions.

## Output
Produce a requirements brief containing:
- Scope, users, business process, and representative questions.
- Requirement table: ID, statement, acceptance example, source/evidence, owner, and status.
- Glossary of disputed or essential terms.
- History, identity, time, quality, and access requirements.
- Decisions, assumptions, exclusions, and unresolved questions.

## Completion checks
Map every proposed model component to a requirement. Do not expand scope with speculative future structures. Do not mark a requirement business-approved without recorded approval. If an unresolved question determines grain or identity, keep the affected model provisional and explain the specific dependency.

## Basis
DAMA-DMBOK2 chapter 5, printed pp. 125–127 and 152–155. Lakehouse-specific questions extend that requirements workflow.

skills.description: Choose the right modeling scheme for a lakehouse product: relational/3NF, dimensional, Data Vault, Anchor, UML, ORM/FCO-IM, or NoSQL/document. Use when starting a subject area, when allocate-medallion-responsibilities needs a scheme decision, or when someone proposes a specialized method.

---
name: select-modeling-scheme
description: >-
  Choose the right modeling scheme for a lakehouse product: relational/3NF,
  dimensional, Data Vault, Anchor, UML, ORM/FCO-IM, or NoSQL/document. Use when
  starting a subject area, when allocate-medallion-responsibilities needs a
  scheme decision, or when someone proposes a specialized method.
---
# Select a modeling scheme

## Inputs
Read the requirements brief, source profile, layer allocation, consumer questions, team skills, existing enterprise conventions, and target platform. Choose per product, not once for the whole lakehouse.

## Candidate schemes and when they fit
| Scheme | Fits when | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Relational / 3NF canonical | Reusable Silver integration, many consumers, strong identity and update rules | Hard for analysts to navigate directly; many joins |
| Dimensional (star, facts and dimensions) | Gold analytics, BI, KPIs, slice-and-dice by conformed dimensions | Needs clear grain; poor for operational integration |
| Data Vault (hubs, links, satellites) | Many volatile sources, full auditable history, frequent source change, parallel loading | Heavy object count and query complexity; usually needs a dimensional layer on top for consumers |
| Anchor modeling (6NF-style, attribute per table) | Highly evolving schemas where nondestructive change and per-attribute temporal history matter most | Extreme table count; tooling and team familiarity are rare |
| UML class modeling | Communicating with application/software teams, object models, inheritance-heavy domains | Not a storage design; translate to relational or dimensional for the lakehouse |
| ORM / FCO-IM (fact-oriented) | Verbalizing business rules with domain experts, validating constraints and n-ary facts before logical design | Conceptual/analysis tool; output still needs mapping to tables |
| NoSQL / document / nested | Collections read together with their parent, semi-structured payloads, Bronze landing, nested Silver child arrays | Weak cross-document joins and constraints; define stable child identity |

## Procedure
1. List the product's main purpose: capture, integration, analytics, communication, or rule validation.
2. Score each candidate against the needs that matter here: history and audit depth, source volatility, number of sources, consumer navigation, query performance, schema-change frequency, and team familiarity.
3. Prefer the simplest scheme that meets the requirements. Specialized schemes (Data Vault, Anchor) need a stated requirement such as auditability across many changing sources; do not adopt them by default.
4. Allow different schemes in different layers, for example document-shaped Bronze, relational or Data Vault Silver, and dimensional Gold. State how data moves between them.
5. Use UML or ORM/FCO-IM as communication and validation notations alongside the chosen storage scheme, not as a replacement for it.
6. Record the decision with requirement-based reasons, rejected alternatives, and the consequences for tooling, team skills, and query complexity.
7. If a specialized scheme is adopted, follow that project's conventions and deeper method documentation for implementation details, and consider writing a focused implementation skill for it.

## Output
A scheme decision record per product: purpose, chosen scheme, layer, reasons, rejected alternatives, and implications for downstream skills.

## Completion checks
Every product has one justified storage scheme. No specialized scheme is chosen without a stated requirement it uniquely serves. Consumer-facing products remain navigable for their users.

## Basis
The source document (DAMA-DMBOK2 chapter 5 skill pack) says these methods inform scheme selection. The fit and caution notes above are general modeling practice added on top, not quoted from the chapter.
